query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing conventional fusion‐based additive manufacturing with a solid‐state, additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) process for AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will overcome residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity in miniature components.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock prepared by mechanical alloying, exhibiting fine-scale compositional homogeneity and a microstructure analogous to other high-entropy alloy powders.
generation.intervention: Implement a low-temperature AFSD process that uses a rotating tool to plastically deform and consolidate the powder feedstock in a layer-by-layer fashion without full melting.
generation.conditions: Build miniature components (feature sizes on the order of a few millimeters) at ambient or moderately elevated substrate temperatures. Use process parameters (tool rotational speed, traverse rate, and applied load) tuned to ensure sufficient plastic deformation while remaining in the solid state. Deposition should be performed in a controlled environment to guarantee process repeatability.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, equiaxed grain structure generated by severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization during solid-state deposition.
generation.mechanism: By avoiding high-temperature melting, AFSD minimizes transient thermal gradients and associated residual tensile stresses. The severe plastic deformation inherent in the process promotes grain refinement and homogenization, which in turn preserves or even enhances yield strength and ductility relative to components fabricated under conventional high-thermal-load regimes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to fusion-based AM parts, components fabricated via AFSD are expected to exhibit markedly lower residual stresses, improved mechanical properties (e.g., higher yield strength and ductility), and reduced processing complexity (less cracking and warpage), thus enabling reliable production of miniature components.
generation.baseline: Components manufactured by conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing methods, which typically suffer from large residual stresses, degraded mechanical performance, and increased process-induced defects.
generation.boundary: The benefits are predicted to apply to miniature-scale components processed with optimized AFSD parameters. The extension to larger or geometrically complex parts may require further process development. In addition, the optimal window depends on achieving sufficient plastic deformation in the solid state without incurring excessive tool wear or incomplete consolidation.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends findings from AFSD studies on Al alloys and high-entropy alloy systems (e.g., evidence from PMC11277587 and PMC12113129) to the AlCrFeNiSi system. The exact parameter window for successful consolidation of this specific powder feedstock is not yet established, and the quantitative improvements in mechanical properties may vary until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components: one set via conventional laser-based fusion AM and another set using the AFSD process with optimized solid-state processing parameters. Ensure both sets are made with similar geometries and build orientations.
measurements: Residual stress distribution by X-ray or neutron diffraction
Microstructural characterization via SEM and EBSD to assess grain size and phase homogeneity
Mechanical testing (tensile tests to determine yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility)
Dimensional accuracy and defect inspection (e.g., porosity, cracking) via appropriate microscopy techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the AFSD-fabricated components do not show a statistically significant decrease in residual tensile stresses and an improvement (or at least maintenance) of mechanical properties compared to the fusion AM components, or if processing complexity (such as defect rates or dimensional inaccuracies) is not demonstrably reduced, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAdditive friction stir deposition (AFSD) is an emerging solid-state additive manufacturing process with a high deposition rate. Being a non-fusion additive manufacturing (AM) process, it significantly eliminates problems related to melting such as cracking or high residual stresses. Therefore, it is possible to process reactive materials or high-strength alloys with high susceptibility to cracking. Although the residual stresses are lower in this process than with the other AM processes, depending on the deposition path, geometry, and boundary conditions, residual stresses may lead to undesired deformations and deteriorate the dimensional accuracy. Thermal cycling during layer deposition, which also depends on the geometry of the manufactured component, is expected to affect mechanical properties. To this day, the influence of the deposit geometry on the residual stresses and mechanical properties is not well understood, which presents a barrier for industry uptake of this process for large-scale part manufacturing. Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) exhibit excellent casting properties and comprehensive mechanical performance, making them suitable for fabricating spatial engineering components using additive manufacturing techniques. However, the rapid solidification process also leads to increased internal stress and reduced structural stability in the components. Therefore, this study focuses on the AlFeCoCrNi2.1 EHEA as the research subject, utilizing laser additive manufacturing to fabricate components and systematically investigating the influence of heat treatment processes on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the components. The research demonstrates that low-temperature heat treatment (700 °C and below) acts as a stress relief-annealing process for the components. The yield strength decreased from 1003.2 MPa to 742.1 MPa. At 900 °C heat treatment, the constraining effect between recrystallized grains and surrounding grains outweighs the dislocation release effect caused by recrystallization, resulting in an increase in dislocation density.
